text: His name was Mahmud of Ghazni. Starting around the year one thousand, he raided north India again and again. About seventeen times.

He came for gold. His raiders stripped cities and temples, including the famous temple of Somnath in Gujarat, in ten twenty-six. Then he went home, his camels loaded. Keep that picture in your mind: India's gold, leaving on someone else's camels.
Mahmud never stayed. But about a hundred and fifty years later, another raider from Afghanistan arrived with a much bigger idea. He didn't just want India's gold. He wanted India.
His name was Muhammad of Ghor. And in eleven ninety-one, at Tarain, near Delhi, he ran into the Rajput king Prithviraj Chauhan.
Prithviraj crushed him. Ghori was badly wounded, and his own men carried him off the field.
Shall we chase them, Your Majesty?
[waving it off] Let them go. A man who loses like that doesn't come back.
Whatever he really said, he didn't finish the job.
A year later, Ghori came back. Same battlefield. A bigger, better-trained army. This time, Prithviraj lost. Rule one of history: if you beat someone, make sure they don't come back next year.
In twelve oh six, one of Ghori's generals became the first sultan of Delhi, and began the tallest brick minaret in the world: the Qutb Minar. You can still see it in Delhi today.
In these same years, Nalanda was sacked, and its great libraries were lost.
And here's where our question really begins. Mahmud came for the gold and went home. These newcomers came for the gold... and stayed.

For the next three hundred years, five different families would rule from Delhi. And they were about to discover that ruling India was very different from robbing it. Especially the strangest sultan of them all.
